definition: Confection means a sweet, elaborately made food.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word confection. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know confection should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The wedding's confection took two days to build and four minutes to disappear.
A snack is far plainer than a confection — grabbed, not made, sweetness with no ambition at all, while a confection is sugar somebody engineered to be admired.
Dessert goes further than a snack — a course in its own right — but it stops short of confection, which is sugar with architecture: built to be admired before it is eaten.

A treat is anything sweet you are glad to get — a candy bar counts, so does one free cookie — and the word says nothing about workmanship. A confection is built: sugar with a blueprint behind it, assembled to be admired before it is eaten. Every confection is a treat; few treats earn the name confection.

A dainty is an old-fashioned word for a choice small sweet — the sort passed around on a tea tray, prized for being delicate and little. A confection can be enormous; what earns that name is not the size of the sweet but the craft and elaborate making behind it.

Confection means a sweet, elaborately made food.

Every December the corner bakery gives its window to one confection: a sleigh of gingerbread and dark chocolate, harnessed to marzipan reindeer with candied-cherry noses, gliding on drifts of royal icing.
Children fog the glass over it all month, and on the twenty-fourth the baker raffles it off for the food pantry.
Confection is the exact word for that sleigh, because a confection is a sweet, elaborately made food — and the stress falls on made.
A treat is anything sweet in the hand; a confection is sugar with a blueprint behind it, food somebody engineered.
Confection is for sweets with craft in them — and, stretched, for anything charmingly over-assembled: a confection of a hat.
A treat is anything nice in the hand; a dessert is a course at the meal's end.
Say confection when the making is the point.

For the final round of the baking show, contestants were given eight hours and one instruction: build a confection worthy of the word.
Dev understood what the judges meant.
A tray of good cookies would not do, however delicious; neither would a bowl of fudge.
The word called for construction — sugar with a plan behind it.
He sketched first: a carousel with pulled-sugar horses, a striped meringue canopy, and a ring of candied orange slices for the platform.
When the judges circled it at last, they spent a full minute admiring the engineering before anyone picked up a fork, which was, Dev thought, exactly the point.
